Anger has no lasting object. As explained earlier, anything that exists is under God's will. If God rejected it completely, it would not exist.

An effect needs its cause not only to begin, but to continue. Each punishment needs anger to continue with it. The first anger may bring someone into Hell, but it does not by itself make the punishment last forever, since anger is a passing state.

This refers to God's words, “My servants who have wronged themselves, do not despair of God's mercy. God forgives all sins,” and to the sacred report quoted here, which also addresses everyone as “My servants.”
This points to the plain where people gather for judgment. A report says that all people will be gathered in one open place.
This is the all-embracing flow of existence, God's creative word “Be.” It is one at the beginning and remains one at the end.

We have said before that the world of forms reached by the body's senses—from the Footstool down to the center of the earth—and the forms of Hell in the next life are joined to the forms of this world. In this sense, they seem not to belong to the next life. What remains there are the forms of Paradise and forms seen through the soul's clear inner sight. The world of meaning is one, because matter, time, place, and the other things that divide bodies are absent there. This oneness remains until it takes form in two worlds of images—one of form, one of matter. They branch out like a person whose two feet come down from one body. This image of the Footstool stands for the universal soul, which includes all souls, both blessed and wretched. The two feet branch out from it because spirit and body are joined.

The Shaykh's words—that the two feet rest in Paradise and Hell—do not conflict with the author's claim that one flow of existence goes to this world and the other to the next. As explained, the forms of Hell belong with the forms of this world. The area from the Footstool to the earth's center shows forms of Paradise when the senses are guided by the intellect and lit by it. It shows forms of Hell when the senses are used without the intellect's guidance. The Shaykh means that both feet come from God, the Giver of peace, and bring peace to those in both homes. They begin with the All-Merciful and end in mercy.
This alludes to God's words: “God created seven heavens, and of the earth the same number. His command descends between them.”
The Persian word means “to set the staff down and rest.” It is a way of speaking about reaching the end of a journey and resting there.
The commentator says Ibn Arabi calls them two groups, though he describes three, because he divides them by whether or not they enjoy complete comfort.
The hardship lasts longer than in the first example, but it eventually ends. These people then live in their home, Paradise.
The phrase “the people of this other home” begins the discussion of those who truly belong in Hell.
The Arabic word means “to be full” or “to be filled.” Hell's pain ends when its fire and fuel increase and fill it. Its pain came from being incomplete.

The mystics say that every being is ruled by one of God's names. The people of Paradise are under gentle names such as “Lord,” while the people of Hell are under “Overpowering.” The word for “Overpowering” can also mean “one who restores what is broken,” as in the prayer, “O Healer of broken bones.”

This answers the idea that God does not care because people are only a handful of dust. If they were so insignificant, He would not punish their crimes, become angry, or act with such force. These are signs that He does care.
This means pairing and sharing. God says, “We created every pair,” such as matter and form, soul and spirit, body and soul, good and evil, light and darkness, and many other pairs.
A person who knows God does not think badly of Him or judge the people of any home in a way that conflicts with God's judgment and will.

The mystics add “servant of” to a divine name for each being that shows that name. Someone who shows knowledge may be called “servant of the All-Knowing”; someone who shows patience, “servant of the Patient”; and one who gives gifts, “servant of the Giver,” even if their given name is Zayd, Amr, or Bakr. Paradise is ruled by the Gentle, Hell by the Overpowering, and the Heights between them by both. The Heights are where a person's good and bad deeds are equal. God also has names made up of more than one name, each with its own effects, such as “the Living, the Self-Sustaining,” “the All-Merciful, the Most Compassionate,” and “the Most High, the Great.”
The pull comes from an inner fit between the person and the place; it is not foreign to their nature. God's name guides them. His power and greatness shine out, and His majesty is also beauty.
The commentator thinks the word means Hell itself, not a promise of punishment. The usual word for a threat of punishment has a different ending.
God's threat, like His promise, reaches everyone in some way. Even Paradise has hardships on the way to it, as the report says, “Paradise is surrounded by hardships.”
It is like being bitten by someone you love, or drinking sweet rosewater.

A mixed thing is never pure, and what is limited is not the unlimited. But this does not mean that anything is truly separate from God. There is no second reality beside existence itself. Whatever we suppose to be a second reality is still that same existence. God says He does not forgive worshipping another god alongside Him. This means that no second reality can stand beside pure existence. Pure existence includes everything of its own kind and leaves out what is foreign to it: a thing's definition and its absence. Yet when the mind, imagination, or senses point to those things, they too have some kind of existence. The word “forgive” can mean “cover,” as when a crowd covers the ground. So the verse means that real existence cannot be covered or surrounded by a second reality. It includes every other distinct thing, whether great or small, but it does not allow a second god.

This raises a question. Direct awareness is said to be the very thing known as it exists outside us. If the thing known is an absence, then awareness would be an absence too, and an absence cannot cause anything. But if, as the author says, it has a kind of existence, how can it be a real evil when existence is good? The answer is that direct awareness does not make pure nothingness present. We cannot picture pure nothingness, such as a complete empty space or the removal of a drawing from a board. What we directly experience is a real state opposite to the thing that is missing. The afterlife images of direct awareness are distorted forms of worldly deeds. The badness of those deeds came from the absences that accompanied them.
We explained this earlier in the section on the divine world, quoting a respected authority. The notes there may help here.

The opening of this chapter says that Hell's true form is the original truth of this world. The ugly forms created when deeds take shape—as painful habits and images—are not its true form, because they actively exist.

The lasting light belongs to God, not to the sun, moon, or stars themselves. A Persian verse says, “How many times has this stream changed its water, while the moon and stars still shine in its reflection.”

Worldly pleasure is mixed with decay and passing away. Its joy carries sorrow; its antidote is poison; its cure is illness; its pleasure is pain. Its forms are constantly breaking apart, and its meetings are only brief contacts. There are many other flaws like these.

If Hell came from the divine name “Overpowering,” rather than from pain, absence, and defect, it would already be complete through God's power. It would not be hungry and thirsty, cry “Is there any more?” or consume itself. It would not be so narrow that God had to place His foot in it. Instead, God brings it wide mercy, giving it more room to ask for more and to act against the tyrants. The Fire's need shows that people are mistaken about how it was made.
This means that worldly deeds prepare the food of the next life.

Deeds create lasting qualities in the soul, and these qualities give rise to forms suited to them—both the food and the form of the person who eats it. Good deeds may make people appear beautiful and youthful in the next life; bad deeds may give them ugly forms, like monkeys or pigs.
This is the careful mystic Ibn Arabi, in chapter 87 of The Meccan Revelations, in his discussion of protecting oneself from the Fire.

He means that the lower world of images is set beneath the high world visible to us. The stars, like glowing embers, affect the high world of Paradise just as fire under a pot affects what is above it. In this way, the heat from the stars also works below them.

His point is that fire is useful both to those in Hell and to the people of Paradise. Its own good for those in Hell has been explained earlier. For Paradise, it ripens its fruit, reshapes the people who live there, gives the ground its scent of musk, and strengthens the roots of its trees.

Heat is a distant cause of these changes. The nearer causes are good habits in the soul and the afterlife changes and improvements that follow from them. The shaping and purification of the soul come from its love of God, its journey toward Him, and its quick progress on that path.
This means the body considered simply as matter. In that sense, it has no touch and cannot feel. But as limbs and organs, bodies can feel pain because they have touch.
“Enjoy completion” means “become more complete.” Body considered as matter has no sense of touch, so it cannot feel pain or pleasure.

These are only secondary qualities of a body. For example, heat is not the completion of water as a kind of body, and cold is not the completion of the heart or liver. Heat and cold are additional qualities for them. A body's division into parts may not be a completion either, since it breaks the body's basic connected form. This may follow from the view that bodies are made of indivisible parts or that their basic extension is both body and matter.

A body considered as matter may lose its connection without pain, because it has no touch. But losing that connection is not a completion for it. It removes what gives its nature unity and leads to its breaking apart. How could a lack of connection be a completion?
The limbs and organs serve the mixed human soul, joined to the animal soul. That is where pain and punishment are felt, as in the case of Hell's keepers.

Saying that the animal soul is not guilty does not mean that it cannot feel pain. Pleasure and pain are the awareness of what suits or harms a being. The animal soul senses particular things that suit or harm it, and each power takes pleasure in what suits it and feels pain at what does not. The sense of touch, for example, enjoys balanced warmth and smoothness, but feels pain from harsh heat or cold and roughness. Taste enjoys sweetness and feels pain at bitterness; the other senses work in the same way. Still, though animals can feel pain, they are not punished by God for it. Their souls feel pain, but not as punishment. They do not have the grief, regret, and inner torment that belong to a higher soul. Those deeper pains belong to the human soul where it is joined to the animal soul.

The rational soul belongs to the highest spiritual realm, and its time is eternal. It is the simple intellect, the spirit of God in the world of meanings. How could the dust of the natural world or its opposites reach it? A Persian verse says: “If you keep measuring yourself as front and back, you are bound to the body and cut off from the soul. Above and below, front and back, are words for the body; the bright soul is beyond direction. Open your sight with the King's pure light, or you will think like someone short-sighted.”
Here the author means the angels who act in the world, the spirits attached to things, and the natures impressed in them.
This explains in detail what he means by “the spirits.”

The fixed stars are beyond number, like grains of sand and drops of sea water, and so are their spirits, or perhaps they are even more numerous. But when they are grouped according to the twelve signs of the zodiac, then together with the spirits of the seven moving planets they make nineteen governors.

This means the Paradise of God's essence and the Paradise of His qualities. The author restates part of his account of spiritual resurrection in a different way, while also giving the passage a fitting end. A strong opening and a strong ending are both valued, as we see in the Qur'an's chapters.

At this stage, the seeker no longer follows personal desire. They want only what God wills and commands, and dislike only what He dislikes and forbids. God's commands express His active will; His prohibitions express, in a secondary way, what He rejects. When personal desire and purpose disappear, so do the needs they create. The seeker becomes rich through God's richness. A Persian verse says: “Everyone has some desire in mind; my desire is to have no desire.”

The weak and uncertain existence of these images is mainly due to the way they serve, in this life, as mirrors in which we see material things. We do not usually attend to them for their own sake. If we did, they would be stronger and more complete, because they are simpler and more lasting. These images show the soul material things; they exist for you, not for matter or for the external object. Without them, you would know nothing of what is outside. People sometimes say that imagined coins, sweets, and similar things are useless. That is true only when they are trying to encourage someone to work for real things. In fact, these images are real creations made by you through a power God gives you. They are also real things outside matter, because they exist in the soul, and the soul is outside matter. An image of something that exists outside the mind is itself a real thing. As explained in discussions of mental existence, what exists in the mind is called “mental” in comparison with material things outside the soul. Considered on its own, without that comparison, it is an external reality. If our worldly interests did not keep us focused on material things, our mental images would not merely reflect those things or be weak. When the soul has few distractions and desires, these images become so strong that they can be mistaken for material things. This is why Ibn Arabi said, “There is no greater confusion in all existence than mistaking imagination for sense perception.”

There is no sequence among these images. They are infinite in number, not spread without end along a single dimension. We quoted a passage from Illuminationist philosophy in our notes on forms that supports this point.
The commentator takes this as Ali saying: “Although I am Adam's son in outward form, my inner meaning bears witness to my spiritual fatherhood.”

In their own view, the people of Hell undergo a change of identity, because they believe they are nothing but their skins, natural powers, and outward forms. Their souls seem to be absorbed into their bodies. The people of truth are the reverse: their bodies are absorbed into their souls, especially those with simple intellectual understanding. This is why a report says that a believer's body does not decay.

This explains how the heavenly spheres and their forces govern people in this world: people are immersed in bodily life, nature, and what follows from them. Their mixtures, compounds, and tastes all depend on the influence of the heavenly spheres. This is the world in which these effects become visible.
This means in their first creation, according to what their earlier deeds call for; and in their continued existence in the next life. They remain stars, but no longer shine or pierce the darkness.
Just as the true Paradise is close to the realm of divine power and the universal intellects, the Paradise of God's qualities is close to the divine realm.

This renewal is like the changes of this world, because the people of Paradise have left the world and its ways. We explained earlier that renewal and expansion belong to the way these separate beings exist.
الحكمة المتعالية في الأسفار العقلية الأربعة
الباب الثامن: في إبطال تناسخ النفوس والأرواح ودفع ما تشبث به أصحاب التناسخ وفيه فصول
٢. في ابطال التناسخ باقسامه والإشارة إلى مذاهب أصحابه وهدم آرائهم
٣. في دفع الشكوك الباقية لأصحاب النقل وحلها
٤. في تتمه الاستبصار لهذا الباب من جهة كيفية نسبه النفس إلى البدن والإشارات إلى الموت الطبيعي واجله والفرق بينه وبين الاجل الاخترامي
٥. في أن لكل شخص انساني ذاتا واحده هي نفسه وهي بعينها الحي
٦. في ضعف ما قاله صاحب المطارحات في هذا المقام دفعا لما قيل في تكثر القوى من غير أن يرجع إلى ذات واحده
٧. في أن هذه القوى البدنية كلها ظل لما في النفس من الهيئات النفسانية
الباب التاسع: في شرح بعض ملكات النفس الانسانية وأفعالها وانفعالاتها ومنازل الانسان
٢. في أوصاف النفس الانسانية ومجامع أخلاقها واختلافها في الشرف والردائة
٣. في منازل الانسان ودرجاته بحسب قوى نفسه
٤. في كيفية ارتقاء المدركات من أدنى المنازل إلى أعلاها والكلام في مراتب التجرد
٥. في أن قوى النفس المتعلقة بالبدن بعضها أقل قبولا للتجزي وبعضها
الباب العاشر: في تحقيق المعاد الروحاني والإشارة إلى السعادة العقلية والشقاوة التي بإزائها والى السعادة والشقاوة الغير الحقيقيتين وما قيل في بيانهما وفيه فصول
٢. في كيفية حصول هذه السعادة ومنشأ احتجاب النفس عنها ما دامت في هذا العالم
٣. في الشقاوة التي بإزاء السعادة الحقيقية
٤. في سبب خلو بعض النفوس عن المعقولات وحرمانهم عن السعادة الأخروية
٥. في كيفية حصول العقل الفعال في أنفسنا
٦. في اظهار نبذ من أحوال هذا الملك الروحاني المسمى عند العرفاء بالعنقاء على سبيل الرمز والإشارة
٧. في بيان السعادة والشقاوة الحسيتين الأخرويتين دون العقليتين الحقيقيتين
٨. في اختلاف مذاهب الناس في باب المعاد
١٠. في تفاوت مراتب الناس في درك امر المعاد وتفاضل مقاماتهم في ذلك
١١. في التنبيه على شرف علم المعاد وعلو مكانه وسمو معرفه بعث الأرواح والأجساد وعظم شانها
الباب الحادي عشر: في المعاد الجسماني وما يرتبط به من أحوال الآخرة ومقاماتها وفيه فصول
١. في ذكر أصول يحتاج إليها في اثبات هذا المقصد أو ينتفع بها فيه
٢. في نتيجة ما قدمناه وثمره ما أصلناه
٣. في دفع شبه المنكرين وشكوك الجاحدين لحشر الأجساد
٤. في القبر الحقيقي وانه روضه من رياض الجنة أو حفره من حفر النيران
٧. في مادة الآخرة وهيولي صورها الباقية
١٠. في أن للنفس الانسانية أنحاء كثيره من الحشر بعضها قبل حدوث هذا البدن الطبيعي وبعضها بعده
١١. في أن للانسان حشرا كثيرا كثره لا تحصى
١٢. في تذكر ان الموت حق والبعث حق
